translationRepairs: In the first year of Shengming, when Shen Youzhi rebelled, Inspector Chen Xianda raised troops in support of the court, and Dun was executed for his earlier complicity.
In the first year of Shengming, when Shen Youzhi rebelled, Inspector Chen Xianda raised troops in support of the court, and Dun was killed for his hesitation.
猶預 means hesitation or indecision. The existing translation incorrectly makes Dun complicit in Shen Youzhi's rebellion.
In the first year of Shengming, when Shen Youzhi rebelled, the inspector Chen Xianda raised troops in response to the court, and Dun was killed for prior involvement.
In the first year of Shengming, when Shen Youzhi rebelled, the inspector Chen Xianda raised troops in response to the court, and Dun was killed for hesitation.
The literal field repeats the same semantic error: 猶預 is hesitation, not prior involvement.
Hui was fearful and alarmed, went to the Founding Emperor to apologize, and was immediately provisionally appointed advisory staff officer on the Heir Apparent's Central Army staff.
Hui was fearful and alarmed, went to the Founding Emperor to apologize, and was immediately provisionally appointed advisory staff officer on Shizu's Central Army staff.
世祖中軍 identifies the Central Army staff of Shizu, the future Emperor Wu, rather than an heir apparent's staff.
When the Heir Apparent acceded, Hui was transferred to Household Subordinate of the Heir Apparent, but did not accept.
When Emperor Wu acceded, Hui was transferred to Household Subordinate of the Heir Apparent, but did not accept.
世祖卽位 refers to Emperor Wu's accession. The Heir Apparent is named only in the office to which Hui was then appointed.

He was transferred to central army staff officer on the Prince of Guiyang's Northern Expedition staff, served on palace duty alongside the future Emperor Wu, won Emperor Ming's personal favor, and thereby became close friends with the Heir Apparent.

He was transferred to central army staff officer on the Prince of Guiyang's Northern Expedition staff, served on palace duty alongside the future Emperor Wu, won Emperor Ming's personal favor, and thereby became close friends with the future Emperor Wu.
Both occurrences of 世祖 refer to the future Emperor Wu, with whom Liu Quan served and became close.
Tan had a handsome beard and whiskers and had old ties with the Heir Apparent, the Prince of Yuzhang.
Tan had a fine beard and whiskers and was on old terms with Shizu, then Prince of Yuzhang.
世祖豫章王 identifies Shizu while he was Prince of Yuzhang, not the Heir Apparent.
When the Heir Apparent did not go west, Quan was appointed Gentleman at the Yellow Gates and acted as administrator of Wu commandery.
When the future Emperor Wu did not go west, Quan was appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and placed in acting charge of Wu Commandery.
世祖 is the future Emperor Wu, and 行吳郡事 means that Quan was placed in acting charge of Wu Commandery.
He sent Crown Prince Wenhuai and Prince Ziliang of Jingling to straighten their dress and pay the respect due their father's old friend.
He sent Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince Ziliang of Jingling to straighten their dress and pay the respect due their father's old friend.
文惠 is the posthumous designation Wenhui. 'Wenhuai' is a romanization error in both the translation and its extracted title claim.
Quan's father Mou had campaigned against Yin Yan and pacified Shouyang without harming anyone; the people were grateful and erected a stele to honor him.
Quan's father Mian had campaigned against Yin Yan and pacified Shouyang without harming the people; the commoners honored him and erected a stele shrine.
勔 is Mian, as the chapter itself correctly renders 劉勔 in s0091. The proposal notices the inconsistency but replaces Mou with another erroneous reading, Kan.
Quan's father Mou had campaigned against Yin Yan and pacified Shouyang, harming no one; the people thanked him and erected a stele in his honor.
Quan's father Mian had campaigned against Yin Yan and pacified Shouyang, harming no one; the people honored him and erected a stele shrine.
The literal field must likewise render 勔 as Mian, not Mou or Kan.
Quan then replaced Wang Jian, Prince of Shixing, as Bearer of the Staff, supervisor of military affairs in Yi and Ning, and Governor of Yi, retaining his rank as general.
Quan then replaced Xiao Jian, Prince of Shixing, as Bearer of the Staff, supervisor of military affairs in Yi and Ning, and Governor of Yi, retaining his rank as general.
In 始興王鑑, 王 is the title 'prince' and 鑑 is the given name of Xiao Jian. It does not form the personal name Wang Jian.
In the first year of Yanxing he again commanded the Right Army.
In Yanxing 1 (AD 494), he again commanded the Right Army.
The received line's 廷興 is a textual error for 延興, as external editions attest. Supplying AD 494 resolves the reign year without inserting unexplained Chinese into the English translation.
